Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event
Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

vignette:
Malia, a 30-year-old parole officer of Pacific Islander background, came to treatment after months of feeling as if a single taste or a sharp look could pull her back into a part of her life she could not quite hold in mind. The trauma she described occurred while she was working as a relief worker in a war zone, moving through damaged streets to bring supplies to a clinic set up in a half-collapsed school. She remembered the heat, the dust, and the constant strain of hearing raised voices in the distance, but what stayed with her most vividly was one morning when she took a drink from a metal cup that had been used in the field kitchen and was struck by a bitter, metallic taste that seemed to belong to the place itself. Around the same period, she saw victims lined up for bandaging, some staring blankly, some crying, and some trying to make themselves small; now, even brief reminders of victims have the same effect on her, making her stomach tighten and her attention lock onto images she does not want to carry.

Since returning home and taking up work as a parole officer, Malia has found that the ordinary texture of daily life can catch her unprepared. In her office, when a client speaks angrily to another staff member, even in a controlled or seemingly reasonable way, she feels an immediate jolt of alarm. She cannot fully explain it to herself, only that raised faces and tightened mouths seem to promise danger, and she becomes watchful in a way that leaves her tense for the rest of the meeting. The same happens outside work, in small exchanges that other people appear to brush off; a calm expression of anger is enough to make her go rigid, her mind already searching for what might happen next. At home, she has also found herself avoiding certain foods and drinks because that same specific taste from the war zone can arrive in a sip or bite without warning, bringing with it a wave of unease that is hard to shake.

What has made the memory especially distressing for Malia is how incomplete it feels. She says there are parts of the event she simply cannot remember no matter how hard she tries, as if the story breaks apart whenever she reaches for it. When she attempts to think it through deliberately, she finds herself pushing it away before she can fully recall it, almost as though some internal pressure makes her stop before the worst parts come into view. She can summon fragments — the cup in her hand, the taste, the victims waiting for help, the sense of a city under strain — but not a smooth sequence. That broken quality has left her feeling frustrated and unsettled, because she suspects she is missing something important, yet each effort to recover the memory leaves her more depleted and less certain of what actually happened.

Over time, Malia began arranging her life around the possibility of being caught off guard. In her parole office, she keeps meals simple and often skips eating at her desk, partly to avoid the taste that can suddenly transport her back, and partly because she does not want to be distracted if a client starts sounding irritated. She has become careful in supervision meetings, scanning faces for anger before words are fully spoken, and this has made her feel constantly on duty even after hours. Friends have noticed that she seems distant when stories involve injured or suffering people, and she has started declining social gatherings where she might be seated near a loud, argumentative table. Her divorce, which she described as already strained before the deployment, became harder to navigate once she began withdrawing from conversation and avoiding anything that might stir up reminders of the victims she used to see in the field. She does not say she is afraid of the memory itself so much as of what might rush in if she lets it surface too clearly: the taste, the faces, and the sense that she is back in the school clinic with no way to steady herself.

By the time she sought help, Malia was worn down by how often these moments were intruding into her working day and narrowing her life. She wanted to understand why a taste, a victim’s face, or an angry voice could still seize her so completely, and why trying to remember the war zone only seemed to make the memory slip further away. What she most hopes for is to feel that she can eat, listen, and work without bracing for the past to break through, and what frightens her most is the idea that the missing pieces of the memory may forever keep her trapped in a version of the event she cannot fully understand.
